title: The ladder of humility (Rule 7)
hook: twelve rungs, from fear of God to a humble love

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hours, prayer stitched through the monk's day. Your line was nothing before prayer. Did you manage to put something down mid-task, even once? Day one thousand one hundred sixteen.

A man is running from his brother. Night comes. He lies down in the open with a stone for a pillow, and he dreams: "behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it." That's Jacob, in Genesis. Benedict reads that dream in chapter seven of his Rule, and sees in it the shape of a humble life. Up and down. Rung by rung. And he counts the rungs: twelve of them, from the bottom step to the top. Today's word: the ladder of humility.

The chapter opens with a line from Jesus: "whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted." Then Benedict turns it into a picture. On Jacob's ladder, he says, we go down by lifting ourselves up, and we go up by humbling ourselves. Backwards from how ladders usually work. The two side rails, he says, are our body and our soul, and God has set the rungs between them. So what are the rungs? The bottom one is to keep the fear of God always before your eyes, never forgetting that God sees. From there they climb through things you can actually do. Not insisting on your own way. Bearing hard things patiently, without walking off. Telling the abbot your hidden thoughts, instead of letting them fester. Being content with the plain, low job. Speaking gently, and not too much. Not being quick to laugh. And the top rung: a humility that shows even in how you walk and stand, quiet, unshowy. Then the payoff. When the monk has climbed all twelve, Benedict says, he'll come to the love of God that casts out fear. He's borrowing John's letter: "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear." Do you see the arc? The ladder starts with fear and ends with love. What began as effort, done out of fear, becomes habit, done out of love. Humility here isn't only a feeling about yourself. It's a set of things you do: getting your own way out of the way, one rung at a time, until love is what's left.

Here's the practice: take one rung. Sit, and breathe slowly. Look at the rungs again. Not insisting on your own way. Bearing something hard without complaining. Speaking gently, and a little less. Taking the plain job without a fuss. One of them will feel like the one you need. Choose it, just for today. Picture where in your day you'll meet it: the meeting, the dishes, the person who always gets under your skin. If you pray, you can ask for help with that one rung. The bell holds the time.
The ladder of humility. Benedict's twelve rungs, climbed by humbling yourself, from the fear of God to a love that casts out fear.
Your line: humility is a ladder. Today, climb your one rung, once. If you miss it, it's still there tomorrow. Day one thousand one hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Benedictine communities read chapter seven of the Rule aloud in turn with the rest, and the twelve steps are used as a way to examine everyday conduct: speech, patience, obedience and the willingness to take the lowest place.

notes: Genesis 28:12 is quoted from 'behold a ladder', after the KJV's 'And he dreamed, and'.
The superlative 'longest chapter' was cut under the claims rule.

Rule 7 paraphrased: Luke 14:11 opening; the ladder (Genesis 28) with descent by exaltation and ascent by humility; the sides as body and soul; twelve degrees; ending in the love of God that casts out fear (1 John 4:18). The steps listed are a selection, not all twelve, and not in strict order; check each summary against the Rule.
'Not being quick to laugh' paraphrases the steps about laughter (Rule 7, tenth step: not quick to laughter); confirm or reword.
'A man is running from his brother' summarizes Genesis 27:41–28:11.

Editor pass: 'humility isn't thinking badly of yourself' contradicted Rule 7's seventh step (believing oneself lower than all), so the teach, myth item and trapdoor now say humility is not only a feeling but a set of practices; fixed the garbled 'something no one in Genesis mentions' and 'climbed by going down'.

Audit pass: no change. Genesis 28:12, Luke 14:11, 1 John 4:18 exact KJV; Rule 7 rails as body and soul, twelve steps and the move from fear to love rechecked (the spoken selection reverses steps 10 and 11, as the earlier note says).
